claims.claim: Westron is equated with English and everything in it translated with differentiation of style for dialect; related tongues become English-related forms (Rohan like Old English, Dale Scandinavian); alien tongues are left alone.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 144 to Naomi Mitchison (25 Apr 1954)
claims.quote: some differentiation of style to represent dialectal differences

claims.claim: In Gondor the Common Speech is spoken in a nobler and more antique style, which the Elves also adopt when they use it.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 144
claims.quote: nobler and rather more antique style

claims.claim: As a story it is good that many things stay unexplained (especially if an explanation exists); Tolkien fears he erred by explaining too much, and readers stuck at the Council of Elrond.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 144

claims.claim: Quenya is built on a Latin basis with Finnish and Greek because they give him phonaesthetic pleasure; Sindarin is devised to resemble British-Welsh because that character fits Celtic-type legends.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 144

claims.claim: The invention of languages is the foundation, the stories were made to provide a world for the languages, a name comes first and the story follows, and the book is largely an essay in linguistic aesthetic.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 165

claims.claim: Only as much 'language' was left in The Lord of the Rings as readers could be expected to stomach — the visible Elvish is a deliberate restraint.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 165
claims.quote: as I thought would be stomached by readers

claims.claim: The sensibility to linguistic pattern affects Tolkien emotionally like colour or music; Gothic taught him aesthetic pleasure in a language for its own sake.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 163 to W.H. Auden (7 Jun 1955)
claims.quote: affects me emotionally like colour or music

claims.claim: A tale of this sort must consult the writer's roots: a man of the North-west sets it in a world with the Shoreless Sea to the West and endless enemy lands to the East.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 163

claims.claim: Tushery is bogus medieval stuff coloured with expletives like tush, pish, zounds; real archaic English is far terser than modern and says things the slack modern idiom cannot.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171 to Hugh Brogan (Sept 1955, unsent draft)

claims.claim: Putting Théoden's thought into modern idiom would be an insincerity, a disunion of word and meaning, because people who think like that do not talk a modern idiom.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171
claims.quote: a disunion of word and meaning

claims.claim: Narrative (not only dialogue) archaism is defended because heroic scenes do not occur in a modern setting; changing the idiom would be like changing helms and hauberks into modern uniforms.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171
claims.quote: helms, shields, hauberks into modern uniforms

claims.claim: 'Helms too they chose' puts the emphasised word in prominent first place without a clutter of empty words, a trick modern English should relearn by example.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171

claims.claim: English's wealth leaves a choice of styles without any risk of unintelligibility, and refusing to use it is a parochialism of time.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 171

claims.feature: Elrond's archaism by grammar and vocabulary
claims.claim: The Gateway summary of the Brogan draft records Tolkien rejecting 'tushery' as applying only to low-quality pastiche rather than real archaic English, with the Théoden passage as his sample.

claims.feature: legends and language share a taste
claims.claim: Legends depend on the language they belong to and a living language on its legends; Esperanto is dead for lack of legends, and Tolkien's legends were invented to match his languages' taste.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 180 to 'Mr Thompson' (14 Jan 1956)

verdicts.trueWording: some differentiation of style to represent dialectal differences
verdicts.note: Letter 144 read raw from the PDF (pypdf text, p.193-194). Quote exact. Every limb on the page: 'equate the Westron or wide-spread Common Speech of the Third Age with English; and translate everything, including names such as The Shire'; 'Languages quite alien to the C.S. have been left alone'; Rohirrim names 'turned ... into forms like (but not identical with) Old English'; Dale and the Long Lake 'more or less Scandinavian in character'.

verdicts.trueWording: nobler and rather more antique style
verdicts.note: Letter 144, p.194: 'especially from Gondor, where it remains spoken in nobler and rather more antique style (a style also usually adopted by the Elves when they use this language)'. Both limbs verbatim, including the Elves adopting it.

Letter 144, p.193: 'As a story, I think it is good that there should be a lot of things unexplained (especially if an explanation actually exists); and I have perhaps from this point of view erred in trying to explain too much, and give too much past history. Many readers have, for instance, rather stuck at the Council of Elrond.' All three limbs verbatim.

Letter 144, p.194: Quenya 'composed on a Latin basis with two other (main) ingredients that happen to give me phonaesthetic pleasure: Finnish and Greek'; Sindarin's changes 'deliberately devised to give it a linguistic character very like ... British-Welsh ... because it seems to fit the rather Celtic type of legends and stories told of its speakers'. Both halves verbatim.

Letter 165 (Houghton Mifflin), p.233: 'The invention of languages is the foundation. The [stories] were made rather to provide a world for the languages than the reverse. To me a name comes first and the story follows.' and 'It is to me, anyway, largely an essay in linguistic aesthetic'. Quote exact; all four limbs present. Source artifact worth recording: this scan's OCR renders 'stories' as 'stones' in that sentence -- a glyph error in this PDF, not a wording difference; the limb is supported either way.

verdicts.trueWording: as I thought would be stomached by readers
verdicts.note: Letter 165, p.233: 'I should have preferred to write in Elvish. But, of course, such a work as The Lord of the Rings has been edited and only as much language has been left in as I thought would be stomached by readers. (I now find that many would have liked more.)' Quote exact; the deliberate-restraint limb is that same sentence restated, with the Elvish antecedent supplied by the preceding line.

verdicts.trueWording: affects me emotionally like colour or music
verdicts.note: Letter 163 to Auden, p.228: 'the sensibility to linguistic pattern which affects me emotionally like colour or music'. Gothic limb same letter: 'I learned Anglo-Saxon at school (also Gothic ... though decisive -- I discovered in it ... for the first time the study of a language out of mere love: I mean for the acute aesthetic pleasure derived from a language for its own sake)'. 'in it' refers to Gothic; confirmed by the later 'Most important, perhaps, after Gothic ...'.

Letter 163, p.228: 'if you want to write a tale of this sort you must consult your roots, and a man of the North-west of the Old World will set his heart and the action of his tale in an imaginary world of that air, and that situation: with the Shoreless Sea of his innumerable ancestors to the West, and the endless lands (out of which enemies mostly come) to the East.' Every limb verbatim.

Letter 171 to Brogan, p.240: 'The proper use of tushery is to apply it to the kind of bogus medieval stuff which attempts (without knowledge) to give a supposed temporal colour with expletives, such as tush, pish, zounds, marry, and the like. But a real archaic English is far more terse than modern; also many of things said could not be said in our slack and often frivolous idiom.' All limbs verbatim, including the three named expletives.

verdicts.trueWording: a disunion of word and meaning
verdicts.note: Letter 171, p.240: 'But there would be an insincerity of thought, a disunion of word and meaning.' Theoden limb is the same passage: 'Theoden would certainly think, and probably say thus shall I sleep better! But people who think like that just do not talk a modern idiom.' All limbs verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: helms, shields, hauberks into modern uniforms
verdicts.note: Letter 171, p.240: introduced explicitly as 'an example of archaism that cannot be defended as dramatic, since it is not in dialogue, but the author's description of the arming of the guests'; 'But such heroic scenes do not occur in a modern setting to which a modern idiom belongs'; 'I can see no more reason for not using the much terser and more vivid ancient style, than for changing the obsolete weapons, helms, shields, hauberks into modern uniforms.' All three limbs verbatim.

Letter 171, p.240: "'Helms too they chose' is archaic ... if mod. E. has lost the trick of putting a word desired to emphasize (for pictorial, emotional or logical reasons) into prominent first place, without addition of a lot of little empty words (as the Chinese say), so much the worse for it. And so much the better for it the sooner it learns the trick again. And some one must begin the teaching, by example." Every limb including 'by example' is verbatim.

Letter 171, p.240: 'Why deliberately ignore, refuse to use the wealth of English which leaves us a choice of styles -- without any possibility of unintelligibility.' The parochialism limb is Tolkien's own label for that refusal, two paragraphs on (p.241): the 20th-c. delusion that contemporary usages have peculiar validity, 'Shake yourself out of this parochialism of time!'

Recovered by route 2: Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20250919220544id_/https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Letter_171 -- full raw HTML, not a summarizer. Summary section: 'He rejects the charge of tushery, since this term properly denotes low-quality pastiches rather than real archaic English. The latter is far terser than modern English, and it is also capable of saying things that cannot be said in the slack and often frivolous idiom of today. Tolkien takes as an example a passage from The King of the Golden Hall', quoting the King's 'Nay, Gandalf!' speech and then discussing 'Theoden's thoughts'. Quote exact; both limbs supported. Note for the chair, not a defect in the claim: this row's 'feature' field reads 'Elrond's archaism by grammar and vocabulary', which does not describe the claim it is attached to.

Letter 180 to 'Mr Thompson', p.250: 'I made the discovery that legends depend on the language to which they belong; but a living language depends equally on the legends which it conveys by tradition'; 'Volapuk, Esperanto, Ido, Novial, &c &c are dead, far deader than ancient unused languages, because their authors never invented any Esperanto legends'; 'I began with language, I found myself involved in inventing legends of the same taste.' Words match one-for-one; the claim's quote string merely drops Tolkien's own scare quotes around 'legends'.
